1	# Task 11: Solar-system explorer with focus on click
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The app is an interactive, stylised solar system explorer on a dark starfield background.
4	
5	Show a glowing central star and at least 6 planets, each at a different orbital distance, with a different size and colour and orbiting the star at a different speed (inner planets faster). At least one planet has a moon orbiting it, and at least one planet has a ring. Draw a thin circular orbit line for each planet. Planets should also spin about their own axis. Use a simple procedural look (colour, gradients or generated textures); do not load external assets from the network.
6	
7	The user can click a planet to focus on it. On focus, the camera smoothly moves (about 1.5 seconds, eased) to a close view of that planet and keeps following it as it orbits, and a DOM info panel appears showing the planet's name, its orbital period in Earth days, and its distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space, or pressing the Escape key, smoothly returns to the overview showing the whole system and hides the panel. In the overview, the user can drag to orbit the camera around the system and scroll to zoom within sensible limits. Add a toggle button labelled 'Pause' that stops and resumes orbital motion, and shows 'Play' while paused.
8	
9	The scene must look correct on first load with no console errors. Expose

content.thinking:
I'll register my own onFrame callback to call app.camera's setPose each frame, basing distance-to-focus and picking calculations on my own tracked camera pose rather than the controller's, since there could be a one-frame lag between them that causes jitter during following.

For the solar system layout, I'm working out stylised orbital distances and speeds for eight planets since real astronomical ratios (like Neptune's 60190-day period vs Mercury's 88) are too extreme to use directly — I'm scaling distances to roughly 7 through 40 scene units and deriving angular speeds from a power-law relationship to the orbital period so outer planets still move visibly slower without being imperceptible.

I'm also setting camera defaults (distance, elevation, zoom limits) so Neptune's orbit stays in view, and figuring out pointer interaction: distinguishing clicks from drags by movement threshold, and picking planets by projecting their centers to screen space with a forgiving hit radius.

For focus behavior, clicking empty space or the sun unfocuses, clicking another planet switches focus, and while focused I'll suppress drag/wheel input to keep things simple. I'm planning the camera transition between overview orbit pose and a focused pose that tracks the planet's live position with an offset based on its radius.

For the focus offset direction, I'll place the camera on the sun-facing side so the planet appears fully lit with the star behind the camera, recomputing the direction each frame as the planet orbits, with a slight azimuth rotation for subtle shading on the surface.

For transitions, I'm using an eased interpolation between a captured starting pose and a live-computed target pose (either the focus view or the overview), blending position and look-at target over about 1.5 seconds. The focused distance metric is just the live distance between camera and planet position, valid even mid-transition, and "focused" state gets set immediately on click so tests waiting a couple seconds should be fine.

Pausing should freeze all simulated motion -- orbits, spins, moons -- while letting camera transitions still run on real time. For the pause button and info panel, I'm overlaying them on the 640x360 canvas: pause button top-left, info panel bottom-right with pointer-events disabled so it doesn't block clicks, plus a small hint text suggesting users click a planet. I'm also setting up a read-only task state exposed on window via a getter so tests can inspect pause state without mutating it directly.

For the starfield, I'm instancing hundreds of tiny emissive spheres across a large shell radius, which means I need to bump up the camera's far plane well beyond default so they're not clipped. For the sun, I'm relying on emissive material plus bloom and a point light rather than adding an extra glow shell, and I want to double check the available APIs for materials, lighting, bloom effects, and primitive/instance creation before continuing.

content.thinking:
I'm planning to draw orbit paths as thin looped lines using an emissive material so they're visible regardless of lighting, falling back to a scaled torus if that's unreliable. For the moon and rings, I'll position each node manually every frame based on world coordinates—moon offset from Earth's position, rings tilted and attached to their planet—rather than relying on parent-child hierarchy.

For spin, setRotation seems to take Euler angles in radians based on the usage pattern I've seen. Now I'm checking what parameters the ring primitive expects, since I'm unsure whether it lies flat in the XY or XZ plane by default.

Rather than rely on a possibly unsupported ring primitive, I'll build a custom annulus geometry for Saturn's rings myself, double-sided with reversed winding on each face so it renders from both angles, with vertex colors for shading.

For the planet surfaces, I'm considering procedural canvas textures—horizontal noise bands mapped by UV v-coordinate—and will test whether the texture.canvas API renders correctly before committing. For lighting I'll try a point light at the sun's position with ambient fill, experimenting with intensity and decay values to see what looks right.

Beyond that, I'm setting a dark space background color, adding a neutral environment for subtle ambient lighting, and scattering emissive-material star instances on a distant shell radius well beyond the camera's max zoom so parallax stays negligible. I'm also confirming that primitive sizes map directly to diameter, so the sun and planets scale correctly, and planning to drive the camera transition with real elapsed time via the frame delta rather than simulation time.

Now I'm working out the click-to-world projection: computing camera-relative basis vectors, transforming the clicked screen point into normalized device coordinates using the field of view and aspect ratio, then converting that into a screen-space radius for hit-testing against each planet, while mapping mouse events through the canvas's bounding rectangle to get accurate click coordinates.

To validate the picking math, I'm thinking of temporarily drawing debug markers at each planet's projected screen position and comparing them against a screenshot, since I can't otherwise verify correctness without a visual check.

I built the solar system explorer in `src/main.ts`. It typechecks, builds, and renders with no console errors. I couldn't send real clicks, drags, scrolls or key presses. - **Scene:** a glowing sun with a corona and bloom, eight planets (Mercury to Neptune), a starfield, and a thin orbit line per planet. Planets differ in size, colour and orbital distance, and inner planets orbit faster. Orbital speeds are compressed, not the real period ratios. Planets spin, and have procedural canvas textures, so there are no external assets. Earth has one moon, Jupiter has two, and Saturn has a three-band ring.
- **Focus:** clicking a planet moves the camera to a close view over about 1.5 seconds, eased, then keeps following the planet. An info panel shows the planet's name, its period in Earth days and its distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space or pressing Escape returns to the overview and hides the panel.
- **Overview controls:** drag to orbit the camera and scroll to zoom, limited to 30–160 units from the star. Both are disabled while a planet is focused.
- **Pause button:** it stops orbits, spins and moons, and its label switches between "Pause" and "Play".
- **Hooks:** `window.__TASK_STATE__` is a read-only getter with `ready`, `focused`, `paused`, `planets` and `cameraDistanceToFocus`. `window.__focusPlanet(name)` and `window.__unfocus()` do what a click on that planet or on empty space does. `window.__EVAL_READY__` is set after the first frame.

I did my own click picking: I project each planet to the screen with the same camera pose I set each frame and pick the nearest one under the cursor. Tiny distant planets get a minimum 9 px hit radius.

At the default view the planets are small on the 640x360 canvas. I zoomed out so Neptune's orbit isn't cut off.
